**Thornwick Water Services – Operations Meeting Transcript**

**Meeting:** Operations Review – March 2020
**Date:** Monday 16 March 2020
**Time:** 09:00 – 11:20
**Location:** Main Control Room, Thornwick Treatment Works
**Chair:** M. Okafor (Operations Manager)
**Present:** R. Patel (Deputy Operations Manager), S. Whitfield (Compliance Officer), J. Doyle (Network Supervisor), A. Hargreaves (Maintenance Lead), K. Bell (Customer Services), T. Nguyen (Water Quality), P. Singh (Finance), L. Carter (Health & Safety)
**Apologies:** D. Evans (Engineering), F. Marchetti (HR)

---

**1. Minutes of Previous Meeting (10 Feb 2020)**

The minutes of the February meeting were approved. Matters arising are covered under the relevant agenda items below. Noted that the action regarding the calibration of the pH probe at the Booster Station (Ref: ACT-2020-014) remains open; a note has been added to the maintenance log.

---

**2. Regulatory Update – Drinking Water Inspectorate (DWI)**

S. Whitfield provided an update on the current regulatory position. Borough of Thornwick Water Services has_regulatory_body Drinking Water Inspectorate. Record status: current.

The DWI completed their routine quarterly sampling audit at the end of February. The Inspectorate’s report was received on 6 March. No formal enforcement action has been taken. The report contains observations on the documentation for the chlorine residual monitoring at the Hilltop Reservoir, but these are categorised as advisory only.

It was confirmed that the current regulatory status is **current** and that no change to the legal framework or supervisory body is anticipated for the remainder of the financial year. The Inspectorate has requested the updated Chemical Risk Assessment for the Craybourne water treatment works by the end of Q2. P. Singh noted that the cost of the external laboratory validation for the new testing regime has been included in the revised budget forecast.

[ACTION] S. Whitfield to circulate the DWI advisory observations to the Water Quality team and to log the receipt of the report in the compliance register. Due: 20 March 2020.

---

**3. Incident Review – Burst Main on Larchwood Avenue (12 March 2020)**

J. Doyle gave a detailed account of the incident. The burst occurred at approximately 04:15 on Thursday 12 March. The main was a 12-inch cast iron pipe, laid circa 1962, located beneath the junction of Larchwood Avenue and Beech Road. The initial report was received via the customer contact centre at 04:22. The standby crew attended site at 04:40 and isolated the affected section by 05:05.

The burst resulted in a loss of supply to 37 properties. A bowser was requested from the regional mutual aid arrangement and was on site by 07:30. The repair was completed at 16:45 the same day. Supply was fully restored by 17:20, following flushing and the taking of the required water quality samples. The results of the chlorine and bacteriological samples were received on 13 March and were satisfactory.

The estimated volume of water lost was approximately 1,400 cubic metres. The cause of the burst is believed to be a combination of ground movement following the recent frost and the age of the pipe. The pipe has been added to the proactive replacement schedule for the next financial year.

M. Okafor asked whether any customers had been affected beyond the initial 37. K. Bell confirmed that 12 further properties had experienced low pressure for a short period, but no formal loss of supply had been recorded for them. A. Hargreaves noted that the repair crew had found the surrounding soil to be wetter than expected, which may indicate a minor leak that had been present for some time. This will be investigated as part of the post-incident review.
The meeting noted that Ms Chen would be undertaking a structured induction programme during April. This would include visits to the water treatment works, the two service reservoirs, and the main pumping station, as well as meetings with the Water Quality, Network, and Customer Services teams. A. Hargreaves suggested that she should also be introduced to the Borough’s elected members at the next Environment and Climate Scrutiny Committee meeting, which is scheduled for 22 April. K. Bell agreed to arrange this.

There was a brief discussion about the practicalities of the handover. J. Doyle noted that several ongoing projects, including the Larchwood Avenue replacement scheme and the new testing regime, would need to be brought to Ms Chen’s attention at an early stage. K. Bell confirmed that a handover pack had been prepared, and that a series of one-to-one meetings had been booked for her first week. S. Whitfield noted that the compliance register and the current list of open actions would be included in the pack.

[ACTION] K. Bell to issue the formal appointment letter to Sarah Chen and to confirm start date and induction schedule. Due: 18 March 2020.

[ACTION] A. Hargreaves to arrange a short welcome briefing for Sarah Chen with the Water Quality team, to be held in the week commencing 30 March 2020. Due: 27 March 2020.

**5. Budget Position – Financial Year 2019/20**

P. Singh presented the latest budget monitoring report, covering the period to the end of February 2020. The overall position showed a projected underspend of approximately £32,000 against the revenue budget, which was broadly in line with previous forecasts. The main areas of variance were as follows:

Sarah Chen was appointed as Operations Manager. Record status: current.

- Energy costs at the water treatment works were running £14,000 lower than budget, partly due to a mild winter and partly due to the recent optimisation of the pumping schedules.
- Chemical costs were £6,500 over budget, reflecting an increase in the unit cost of ferric sulphate from the supplier. P. Singh noted that the contract was due for retender in the autumn, and that the procurement team had been asked to obtain quotes from alternative suppliers.
- Staffing costs showed a small underspend of £4,200, mainly as a result of the vacancy in the Operations Manager post. This would be offset in the next financial year by the new appointment.
- Reactive maintenance expenditure was £9,800 over budget, driven by the burst on Larchwood Avenue and by two smaller leaks in February. J. Doyle noted that the cost of the emergency repair had been estimated at £7,300, including labour, materials, and plant hire.

M. Okafor asked whether there were any risks that could affect the final outturn. P. Singh noted that the main risk was the possibility of further bursts during the remainder of March, particularly if there was a return to frosty weather. He also noted that the cost of the external laboratory validation for the new testing regime had been included in the revised forecast, as previously discussed. The current projection of a £32,000 underspend was considered to be realistic, with a potential range of between £20,000 and £45,000.

The meeting agreed that no virement was required at this stage. P. Singh confirmed that the final outturn for the year would be reported to the Borough Council’s Finance and Performance Committee in June.

**6. Water Quality Update – New Testing Regime**

S. Whitfield reported that the implementation of the new testing regime was progressing to plan. The additional sampling points had been identified, and the schedule for the first full month of operation under the new arrangements had been circulated to the Water Quality team. The new regime would increase the number of routine samples taken each week from 48 to 64, with additional samples to be taken at the service reservoirs and at selected points on the distribution network.
A. Barnes asked whether the public would notice any change. S. Whitfield explained that the additional sampling was for operational monitoring only and would not affect supply or customer communications. The only visible change would be the appearance of a few more white-topped sample bottles at the service reservoirs, which had already been sighted by residents near the Ridgeway reservoir. No complaints had been received.

He noted that the post had reported to S. Whitfield since the start of the new arrangements, and that this had worked well during the implementation of the new testing regime.

S. Whitfield confirmed that James Okafor lead_water_quality_since 2020-03-16 date, and that the reporting line to her had been in place from that date. M. Okafor noted that the previous interim arrangement, under which the Water Quality Lead had reported to the Operations Manager, had been superseded by the new structure. M. Okafor asked whether there were any staffing concerns in the Water Quality team ahead of the Easter period. S. Whitfield said the team was at full strength, with the exception of one technician who was due to go on maternity leave in May. A temporary cover arrangement was being discussed with HR, and a job description had been drafted. J. Okafor said the cover would be needed for the sampling rounds and for lab support, and that the team could manage with a part-time appointment for the summer period.

P. Singh noted that the cost of the temporary cover had not been included in the current year’s forecast, as it would fall in the next financial year. He asked that the estimate be provided to him by the end of the month so that it could be included in the budget planning for 2020/21.
J. Okafor said the chamber on Mill Lane was on the list for the summer jetting programme anyway, but that the notice meant it would need to be brought forward. He said he had already spoken to R. Hussain, and the jetting crew could be on site the week commencing 19 June. The CCTV survey would need to be booked with the external contractor, and he asked whether the contract was still in place. A. Barnes confirmed that the framework agreement with the contractor ran until September and that the booking could be made through the usual route.

R. Hussain said the crew had inspected the chamber informally on 9 June, and that the standing water appeared to be from a blocked gully rather than a collapse. He said the debris was mostly leaf litter and silt, which was consistent with the location at the bottom of the hill. He cautioned that there might be a root intrusion at the joint near the inlet, but that this could not be confirmed without the CCTV survey. He said he would update the job sheet with the preliminary findings and would arrange for the jetting to be done in advance of the survey so that the camera could get a clear run.

P. Singh asked whether there were any cost implications arising from the notice, and whether the jetting and survey were within the existing maintenance budget. J. Okafor said the jetting was routine and covered by the existing contract, and that the CCTV survey would be an additional cost of approximately £1,200. P. Singh said that was within the contingency line for network maintenance, and that he would need a purchase order number before the survey was booked. J. Okafor said he would raise the requisition by the end of the week.

M. Okafor asked whether the notice would have any bearing on the annual performance report or on the inspection regime carried out by the Drinking Water Inspectorate. A. Barnes said the notice was a separate matter from the DWI regime, but that it would be referenced in the next quarterly compliance summary. He said the Environmental Health Department had been cooperative in the past, and that as long as the works were completed and the response sent, the matter would be closed out without further escalation.

M. Okafor: And what was the immediate response?

A. Barnes: We did three things straight away. First, we isolated the section of main between the reservoir outlet and the first branch to Ash Grove. Second, we issued a customer notice – that went out via the usual channels, text and email to registered account holders, and we put a banner on the website. Third, we started flushing from the hydrant at the bottom of Westfield Road to pull the affected water through and out of the system.

P. Singh: How long did the flushing take?

A. Barnes: We flushed continuously for about six hours on day one, then intermittently for another three hours the following morning. By Tuesday afternoon, we were getting stable readings below 0.5 mg/l at all three of the original properties and at the two additional sample points we'd set up on Ash Grove. We lifted the isolation on Tuesday evening, and the customer notice was withdrawn on Wednesday morning.

M. Okafor: So is this closed out?

A. Barnes: No, not yet. The operational response is complete, but the investigation is still open. We've got the results back from the lab on the samples we took from the reservoir outlet, and we're waiting on two more from the flushing points. The initial hypothesis is that there was a dosing fault at the reservoir – the chlorine analyser was reading low, and the dosing pump had been ramped up manually by the day shift on the Friday before the incident. The analyser was later found to be faulty, so the pump was over-dosing without the safety cut-out kicking in.

P. Singh: So the analyser fault caused the over-dosing?

A. Barnes: That's the working theory, but we've not confirmed it yet. The analyser has been sent away for calibration and fault testing, and the pump has been taken out of service and replaced with a spare. We're also reviewing the SCADA logs to see if there were any alarms that were missed or acknowledged but not acted on. That's part of the investigation, not the immediate fix.

**P. Singh:** Let's pick up where we left off. We were on the cause of the chlorine spike. Jake, you had something more from the SCADA logs?

**J. Whitfield:** Yes. It's not what we first thought. The high chlorine reading wasn't a dosing fault or a valve issue. **1. Minutes of Previous Meeting (10 Feb 2020)**

The minutes of the February meeting were approved. Matters arising are covered under the relevant agenda items below. Noted that the action regarding the calibration of the pH probe at the Booster Station (Ref: ACT-2020-014) remains open; a note has been added to the maintenance log.

---

**2. Regulatory Update – Drinking Water Inspectorate (DWI)**

S. Whitfield provided an update on the current regulatory position. Borough of Thornwick Water Services has_regulatory_body Drinking Water Inspectorate. Record status: current.

The DWI completed their routine quarterly sampling audit at the end of February. The Inspectorate’s report was received on 6 March. No formal enforcement action has been taken. The report contains observations on the documentation for the chlorine residual monitoring at the Hilltop Reservoir, but these are categorised as advisory only.

It was confirmed that the current regulatory status is **current** and that no change to the legal framework or supervisory body is anticipated for the remainder of the financial year. The Inspectorate has requested the updated Chemical Risk Assessment for the Craybourne water treatment works by the end of Q2. P. Singh noted that the cost of the external laboratory validation for the new testing regime has been included in the revised budget forecast.

[ACTION] S. Whitfield to circulate the DWI advisory observations to the Water Quality team and to log the receipt of the report in the compliance register. Due: 20 March 2020.

---

**3. Incident Review – Burst Main on Larchwood Avenue (12 March 2020)**

J. Doyle gave a detailed account of the incident. The burst occurred at approximately 04:15 on Thursday 12 March. The main was a 12-inch cast iron pipe, laid circa 1962, located beneath the junction of Larchwood Avenue and Beech Road. The initial report was received via the customer contact centre at 04:22. The standby crew attended site at 04:40 and isolated the affected section by 05:05.

The burst resulted in a loss of supply to 37 properties. A bowser was requested from the regional mutual aid arrangement and was on site by 07:30. The repair was completed at 16:45 the same day. Supply was fully restored by 17:20, following flushing and the taking of the required water quality samples. The results of the chlorine and bacteriological samples were received on 13 March and were satisfactory.

The estimated volume of water lost was approximately 1,400 cubic metres. The cause of the burst is believed to be a combination of ground movement following the recent frost and the age of the pipe. The pipe has been added to the proactive replacement schedule for the next financial year.

M. Okafor asked whether any customers had been affected beyond the initial 37. K. Bell confirmed that 12 further properties had experienced low pressure for a short period, but no formal loss of supply had been recorded for them. A. Hargreaves noted that the repair crew had found the surrounding soil to be wetter than expected, which may indicate a minor leak that had been present for some time. This will be investigated as part of the post-incident review.

**5. Budget Position – Financial Year 2019/20**

P. Singh presented the latest budget monitoring report, covering the period to the end of February 2020. The overall position showed a projected underspend of approximately £32,000 against the revenue budget, which was broadly in line with previous forecasts. The main areas of variance were as follows:

Sarah Chen was appointed as Operations Manager. Record status: current.

- Energy costs at the water treatment works were running £14,000 lower than budget, partly due to a mild winter and partly due to the recent optimisation of the pumping schedules.
- Chemical costs were £6,500 over budget, reflecting an increase in the unit cost of ferric sulphate from the supplier. P. Singh noted that the contract was due for retender in the autumn, and that the procurement team had been asked to obtain quotes from alternative suppliers.
- Staffing costs showed a small underspend of £4,200, mainly as a result of the vacancy in the Operations Manager post. This would be offset in the next financial year by the new appointment.
- Reactive maintenance expenditure was £9,800 over budget, driven by the burst on Larchwood Avenue and by two smaller leaks in February. J. Doyle noted that the cost of the emergency repair had been estimated at £7,300, including labour, materials, and plant hire.

M. Okafor asked whether there were any risks that could affect the final outturn. P. Singh noted that the main risk was the possibility of further bursts during the remainder of March, particularly if there was a return to frosty weather. He also noted that the cost of the external laboratory validation for the new testing regime had been included in the revised forecast, as previously discussed. The current projection of a £32,000 underspend was considered to be realistic, with a potential range of between £20,000 and £45,000.

The meeting agreed that no virement was required at this stage. P. Singh confirmed that the final outturn for the year would be reported to the Borough Council’s Finance and Performance Committee in June.

**6. Water Quality Update – New Testing Regime**

S. Whitfield reported that the implementation of the new testing regime was progressing to plan. The additional sampling points had been identified, and the schedule for the first full month of operation under the new arrangements had been circulated to the Water Quality team. The new regime would increase the number of routine samples taken each week from 48 to 64, with additional samples to be taken at the service reservoirs and at selected points on the distribution network.

M. Okafor: And what was the immediate response?

A. Barnes: We did three things straight away. First, we isolated the section of main between the reservoir outlet and the first branch to Ash Grove. Second, we issued a customer notice – that went out via the usual channels, text and email to registered account holders, and we put a banner on the website. Third, we started flushing from the hydrant at the bottom of Westfield Road to pull the affected water through and out of the system.

P. Singh: How long did the flushing take?

A. Barnes: We flushed continuously for about six hours on day one, then intermittently for another three hours the following morning. By Tuesday afternoon, we were getting stable readings below 0.5 mg/l at all three of the original properties and at the two additional sample points we'd set up on Ash Grove. We lifted the isolation on Tuesday evening, and the customer notice was withdrawn on Wednesday morning.

M. Okafor: So is this closed out?

A. Barnes: No, not yet. The operational response is complete, but the investigation is still open. We've got the results back from the lab on the samples we took from the reservoir outlet, and we're waiting on two more from the flushing points. The initial hypothesis is that there was a dosing fault at the reservoir – the chlorine analyser was reading low, and the dosing pump had been ramped up manually by the day shift on the Friday before the incident. The analyser was later found to be faulty, so the pump was over-dosing without the safety cut-out kicking in.

P. Singh: So the analyser fault caused the over-dosing?

A. Barnes: That's the working theory, but we've not confirmed it yet. The analyser has been sent away for calibration and fault testing, and the pump has been taken out of service and replaced with a spare. We're also reviewing the SCADA logs to see if there were any alarms that were missed or acknowledged but not acted on. That's part of the investigation, not the immediate fix.

Incident Report IR-2023-014 incident_type chlorine_contamination. Record status: historical.

M. Okafor: And what about the residents? Any health concerns?

A. Barnes: We've had no reports of illness, and at the levels we saw, the health risk is low – it's an aesthetic and taste issue more than a safety one. But we've advised anyone with health concerns to contact their GP and to let us know if they want to be contacted by our water quality team. We've had two families take us up on that so far, and both have been contacted.

P. Singh: Have we had any complaints from residents about the notice itself – timing or content?

A. Barnes: A few. One resident on Ash Grove said they didn't receive the text until two hours after the notice went up on the website, and another said the email link to the FAQ page was broken. The first issue is a known limitation with the SMS provider – there's a delay on some networks – and the second was a typo in the URL. Both have been noted in the incident log as lessons learned. We're not going to change the provider over this, but we will double-check the links before sending next time.

M. Okafor: What about the DWI? Have they been informed?

A. Barnes: Yes. I spoke to the inspector on Tuesday morning, and I sent over a preliminary summary of the incident, the actions taken, and the initial sample results. They've asked to be kept informed of the investigation outcome, and they've also asked for a copy of the SCADA review when it's complete. There's no suggestion of a formal investigation at this stage, but they want to see the root cause analysis before deciding whether any further action is needed.

P. Singh: And the customer notice – is that the same as a 'do not drink' notice?

The customer service team logged it at 09:47. At 09:55, we had a second call from a different resident, same area, same complaint. That's when the duty officer contacted me. I was on site by 10:20.

**Operations Meeting Transcripts – 2 November 2023 (continued)**

**Attendees:** P. Singh (Chair, Water Services Manager), A. Barnes (Operations Supervisor), M. Okafor (Compliance Officer), J. Whitfield (SCADA / Systems Technician), R. Hussain (Maintenance Lead), T. Bell (Customer Services), L. Novak (Finance, joined 11:40), S. Patel (Field Technician, joined 11:35)

**Location:** Thornwick Borough Council, Committee Room 2, and via Teams for field staff.

**Time:** 11:00 – 12:30 (meeting continued from previous session; incident review item carried over).

---

**P. Singh:** Let's pick up where we left off. We were on the cause of the chlorine spike. Jake, you had something more from the SCADA logs?

**J. Whitfield:** Yes. It's not what we first thought. The high chlorine reading wasn't a dosing fault or a valve issue. The data shows the chemical dosing pump at Ash Grove started running continuously from around 02:50, not cycling as it should. The controller was sending a "run" signal, but the feedback loop that should have stopped it at the set point wasn't responding. We think it's the old PLC card – the one we flagged as intermittent back in June. It's been on the replacement list for a while.

**A. Barnes:** So it's a control system failure, not a mechanical one. That changes the narrative a bit.

**J. Whitfield:** It does. The pump itself is fine. The chlorine tank level is fine. It's the logic controller that failed in a way that made the pump run at full stroke. The high alarm did trigger, but the alarm notification didn't get out. We're still checking the notification routing. The automatic acknowledgment at 03:47 – that's the system's own fail-safe, which clears the alarm if it's not manually acknowledged within a set time. It's not designed to be a "silence" – it just logs it as acknowledged. So the alarm was effectively invisible until the morning shift came in.

**P. Singh:** And the PLC card – when was it last tested?

**R. Hussain:** We did a routine check on the 30th of September. It was showing intermittent faults on the output channel. I logged it for replacement, but the part was on backorder. It came in last week – it's actually in the stores now. We just hadn't scheduled the swap.

**P. Singh:** Right. So we have a known faulty component, a delayed replacement, and an alarm notification failure. That's a series of issues. Let's make sure the report to the regulator reflects all three. The cause is the PLC card failure, the contributing factors are the delayed replacement and the alarm routing fault. The completion date for the incident file – we agreed on the 20th of October, when the replacement pump was fully operational and the water quality parameters returned to normal. That's the date we use in all the paperwork.

**M. Okafor:** I'll log that as the formal completion date. That matches the SCADA data and the sampling results from the 20th. The incident file will be updated to show the status as "Closed – Remediated" with that date.

**P. Singh:** Good. Now, let's move to the next item on the agenda – the routine reservoir inspection programme for the winter period. Rob, you had the schedule?

**R. Hussain:** Yes. We've got six covered service reservoirs and two open ones. The winter inspection cycle starts on the 13th of November. We're prioritising the covered ones first because of the cold weather – we want to check the roof hatches and vents are sealed properly before the frost sets in. The schedule is:

**A. Barnes:** Are we doing the internal inspections on the covered ones, or just the external?

**R. Hussain:** Internal for the covered ones – we need to check the water level and look for any cracks or leaks. We'll do a confined space entry for Highfields and Easton, because they're the deeper ones. We've got the permits ready. The team will need to do the gas testing before entry. We'll have two-person teams for each site.

**P. Singh:** What's the proposed fix?
